answer: Assign every newcomer a survey square where a lagoon meets a grove, holding one buried relic. The newcomer maps the square, then digs its layers in order: each layer is photographed in place and catalogued before the next is unsealed, each report sealing the next permit. A laboratory dates the finds. One identity costs one square, 50 hours of sequential fieldwork, and $340 in charges. A farm chasing 10,000 clones owes 10,000 squares and 500,000 hours; squares are lottery-issued and non-transferable, so buying permits creates no new square, and no crew digs two layers at once.
